intro: At C1 you lifted your key words, paused for effect and moved the stress to change what a sentence means. Now your voice carries your attitude: real praise or sarcasm, doubt with a hidden 'but', surprise, boredom or warmth. You'll also learn to hear those attitudes in other people and to fit your delivery to your audience. One honest note: the app's recordings are one calm voice reading plain text, so it can't sound sarcastic or doubtful. The tunes are written in the notes, you say them out loud, and the videos at the end give you real voices.
teachingNotes: Builds on b1-pron-rhythm-intonation (arrows ↗ ↘ →, a wide range for surprise, flat = bored), b2-pron-intonation-attitude (the fall-rise ↘↗ for doubt and a hidden 'but': Really…? ↘↗ = Masa sih…?; a gentle rise for polite requests; contrastive stress I said TUESday, not THURSday; sarcasm only as a recognise-it note) and c1-pron-prosody (pitch range: step up on new information and both sides of a contrast, old information low; pausing for effect; meaning-changing stress I didn't say HE took the money). Recap in a line; don't re-teach. New here: producing attitudes on purpose (real praise vs sarcasm, doubt and reservation with a fall-rise on a stressed word, surprise, boredom, warmth), the link between contrastive stress and attitude (a stressed word + fall-rise points to a contrast that isn't said: The FOOD was nice… ↘↗ = something else wasn't), the cues for hearing attitude, and adapting delivery to the audience. Notation: CAPITALS = stressed word; ↗ rise; ↘ fall; ↗↘ rise-fall; ↘↗ fall-rise; → flat; Gre-eat = drawn out; | = pause.

Attitudes: real praise or enthusiasm = lively, wide range, a high peak and a rise-fall on the key word (GREAT! ↗↘). Sarcasm = the words say the opposite of what you mean; very often flat, low, narrow and drawn out (Gre-eat. →, Su-ure. →), a deadpan style especially common in British English; some speakers do the opposite and exaggerate wildly. The surest clue is that the words don't fit the situation. Doubt or reservation = a fall-rise on the stressed word (It MIGHT work… ↘↗ = but I doubt it; I LIKE it… ↘↗ = but…). Surprise = fast, a big jump up (You're moving to BALi?! ↗). Boredom / disinterest = narrow, flat, low and short (Oh. → Nice. →). Warmth = start a little higher, move gently, don't rush, soft fall; a smile is audible. Node common errors: the same flat 'Great.' for praise and for sarcasm; equal stress on every word ('I DIDN'T SAY SHE TOOK IT') instead of the contrast word ('I didn't say SHE took it' = someone else did); a falling tone on a doubtful statement, so it sounds certain. Advise against sarcasm at work with people you don't know well, with international audiences and in writing; polite doubt (a fall-rise plus might, quite, in theory) is the safer professional tool.

Indonesian traps: Indonesian is usually spoken in a narrower, flatter range, and attitude is carried by words and particles (kok, sih, deh, lho, masa, -lah). Carried into English, a sincere 'Great.' or 'Congratulations.' said flat can sound bored or even sarcastic by accident. Many learners also end statements with a rise, which sounds unsure or like a question (as if asking permission): end with a clear fall when sure. Learners fear a wide range sounds 'lebay'; to English ears it usually sounds engaged and friendly. Indonesian 'Bagus sih… tapi…' maps onto the English fall-rise: the tune does the work of sih and the unsaid tapi.

Hearing attitude: listen to how, not only what. Cues: pitch range (wide = engaged; narrow and flat = bored, tired or sarcastic); length (a drawn-out key word: sarcasm, doubt or strong feeling); the end of the tune (a clear fall = finished and sure; a fall-rise = unfinished, a 'but' is coming); a pause before a word ('It's… | interesting' = searching for a polite word = reservation); a stressed word that sets up a contrast; and the match between words and situation (a positive word about a bad situation = sarcasm, the strongest clue). Use several cues together: a flat voice can simply mean tiredness or an accent. If unsure, ask kindly. In writing all these cues disappear, so 'Great, thanks.' in an email can be read either way.

Adapting delivery: five controls are pace, volume, pausing, articulation (clear sounds and word endings) and formality of voice. Always slow down for key numbers, names and the main point, with a short pause before them. Small meeting: conversational pace and volume. Big hall: slower, longer pauses, wider range and clearer stresses; steady distance from the microphone, no shouting. Non-native / international audience: a little slower, clear word endings, full forms (going to, not gonna), fewer idioms and no sarcasm; this is not talking down. Phone: slower and clearer, numbers in small groups (0812 | 5567 | 3490), spell names with words (S for Surabaya), warmth in the voice. Video call: a small delay, so pause longer before and after questions and let one person talk at a time. Child: slower, simpler, warm and lively. Elderly person: slower, clearer, a bit louder and slightly lower in pitch if they hear poorly (high frequencies usually go first with age), face them; never baby talk or shouting. Indonesian trap: nerves make presenters speed up, drop word endings and flatten their range.

Audio limits and scope: every recording is read once by one natural TTS voice from plain text. It CANNOT produce sarcasm, doubt, a fall-rise, a chosen stress or a chosen tone, so spoken English (tiles, examples, listen) is plain spelling, and notation appears only in notes, prompts and options. Listening questions test only what comes from the words (a positive word about a bad situation = sarcasm; which detail to correct). If the learner asks to hear the difference, describe it (lift your hand on the stressed word; down, then up) and point to the resources, which are real recordings; ask them to record themselves. Many attitude and delivery choices are style and vary by speaker and region: say so, and test only clear cases. Don't teach tone-unit theory (nucleus, key, termination) or regional melodies.

keyPoints.title: Let your voice carry the attitude
keyPoints.explanation: Real praise is lively, with a wide rise-fall on the key word (GREAT! ↗↘). Sarcasm is often flat, low and drawn out (Gre-eat. →). Doubt, or a hidden 'but', is a fall-rise on the stressed word (It MIGHT work… ↘↗). Surprise is a fast jump up, boredom is narrow and flat, and warmth is a little higher, gentle and unhurried. A falling tone on a doubtful sentence makes it sound sure.

examples.id: Hebat! Kita dapat kontraknya. (pujian tulus: GREAT! ↗↘, lebar dan hidup)
Mungkin saja berhasil. (It MIGHT work… ↘↗ = tapi aku ragu)

id.title: Biarkan suaramu membawa sikapmu
id.explanation: Pujian tulus terdengar hidup, dengan nada naik-turun yang lebar di kata kuncinya (GREAT! ↗↘). Sarkasme sering datar, rendah dan diucapkan panjang (Gre-eat. →). Ragu, atau ada 'tapi' yang tidak diucapkan, ditunjukkan dengan nada turun-naik di kata yang ditekan (It MIGHT work… ↘↗). Terkejut = lompatan cepat ke atas, bosan = sempit dan datar, hangat = sedikit lebih tinggi, lembut dan tidak terburu-buru. Nada turun di kalimat yang ragu membuatnya terdengar yakin.

keyPoints.title: Hear the attitude: listen to how, not only what
keyPoints.explanation: Listen for the pitch range (wide = engaged; narrow and flat = bored or sarcastic), the length of key words (Su-ure), the end of the tune (a fall = sure; a fall-rise = a 'but' is coming), a pause before a word (It's… | interesting), a stressed word that sets up a contrast, and whether the words fit the situation. Use several cues together.

examples.id: Menarik. (It's… | INteresting ↘↗: jeda dan nada turun-naik = sopan, tapi tidak yakin)
Makanannya enak sih. (The FOOD was nice… ↘↗ = ada hal lain yang tidak enak)

id.title: Dengarkan sikapnya: perhatikan caranya, bukan hanya kata-katanya
id.explanation: Perhatikan rentang nada (lebar = antusias; sempit dan datar = bosan atau menyindir), panjang kata kunci (Su-ure), akhir nadanya (turun = yakin; turun-naik = ada 'tapi'), jeda sebelum sebuah kata (It's… | interesting), kata yang ditekan untuk menunjukkan kontras, dan apakah kata-katanya cocok dengan situasinya. Pakai beberapa petunjuk sekaligus.

keyPoints.title: Fit your delivery to the audience
keyPoints.explanation: Adjust your pace, volume, pausing, articulation and formality. Slow down for key numbers, names and your main point. Speak more slowly, with longer pauses, in a big hall, to a non-native audience and on the phone; pause longer on video calls because of the delay; speak slowly and warmly to a child, and slowly and clearly to an elderly person, without shouting or baby talk.

examples.en: Our budget for next year is four point two billion rupiah.
examples.id: Anggaran kami untuk tahun depan empat koma dua miliar rupiah. (angka kunci lebih lambat: … is | four point two BILLion rupiah)

examples.en: That's Sari, S for Surabaya, A, R, I.
examples.id: Itu Sari, S untuk Surabaya, A, R, I. (di telepon: pelan, eja nama dengan kata)

id.title: Sesuaikan cara bicaramu dengan audiens
id.explanation: Atur tempo, volume, jeda, kejelasan pengucapan dan tingkat formalitas suaramu. Perlambat untuk angka, nama dan poin utama. Bicara lebih pelan, dengan jeda lebih panjang, di aula besar, untuk audiens yang bukan penutur asli, dan di telepon; beri jeda lebih lama di video call karena ada delay; bicara pelan dan hangat kepada anak, serta pelan dan jelas kepada orang lanjut usia, tanpa berteriak atau bicara seperti kepada bayi.

guidedPractice.prompt: Your colleague Dimas tells you he's just been promoted, and you're really happy for him. You say 'That's great!' Should your pitch range be wide or narrow? Write one word.
guidedPractice.hint: Real praise is lively: a wide rise-fall on the key word, THAT'S GREAT! ↗↘. Narrow and flat sounds bored, or even sarcastic.

guidedPractice.prompt: Pak Hasan is completely sure the product launch will go well. He says 'It WILL work.' Should his voice end with a fall or a fall-rise? Write one word.
guidedPractice.hint: A clear fall ↘ means finished and sure. A fall-rise ↘↗ would add a hidden 'but', which is the opposite of what he means.

guidedPractice.prompt: Budi shows his new business idea to a senior colleague, who answers: 'It's… | INteresting ↘↗' (a pause before the word, then a fall-rise). Is the colleague enthusiastic or unconvinced? Write one word.
guidedPractice.hint: The pause shows the speaker is searching for a polite word, and the fall-rise leaves a 'but' unsaid.

guidedPractice.prompt: You're explaining a form to your elderly neighbour, who doesn't hear high sounds well. Besides speaking a little louder and more slowly, should you make your voice a little higher or a little lower? Write one word.
guidedPractice.hint: With age, high sounds are usually the first to become hard to hear, so a slightly lower voice carries better. Don't shout.

independentPractice.prompt: You tell a colleague some exciting news about your team. He answers 'Yeah. Nice.' in a narrow, flat, low voice and keeps looking at his phone. What attitude do you hear? Write one word.
independentPractice.hint: Narrow, flat, low and short (Yeah. → Nice. →) sounds bored or uninterested.

independentPractice.prompt: On a video call with a client in Makassar there's a small delay. After you ask a question, should you keep talking or wait in silence for a moment? Write talk or wait.
independentPractice.hint: The delay means the answer arrives late. Pause a little longer, and let one person speak at a time.

assessment.prompt: Bu Ani announces that the team meeting has been moved to Saturday morning. Sari says: 'Wo-onderful. →' in a low, flat, drawn-out voice. Which attitude does her delivery show? Choose one from this list and write it: delighted, sarcastic, surprised.
assessment.rubric: Correct: sarcastic (a positive word said low, flat and drawn out about bad news, a Saturday meeting: she means the opposite). 'annoyed' or 'unhappy' = 80 (her real feeling, but the attitude from the list is sarcastic). 'delighted' = 0 (that needs a lively, wide rise-fall: WONderful! ↗↘). 'surprised' = 0 (that's a fast, big jump up ↗).

assessment.prompt: Dimas asks Pak Hasan: 'Will the client sign the contract this week?' Pak Hasan answers: 'I SUPPOSE so… ↘↗' (down on SUPPOSE, then up at the end). How does he feel about it? Choose one from this list and write it: certain, doubtful, delighted.
assessment.rubric: Correct: doubtful (the fall-rise ↘↗ leaves a 'but' unsaid: maybe, but I'm not sure; I suppose so with a fall-rise is reluctant, doubtful agreement). 'reluctant' or 'hesitant' = 80 (close: he agrees without conviction). 'certain' = 0 (that needs a clear fall ↘, as in I'm SURE they will. ↘). 'delighted' = 0 (that needs a lively, wide range).

assessment.prompt: Rina's manager asks if she can join the client dinner on Friday. She'd like to, but she isn't sure she can finish her work in time, and she wants him to hear that hidden 'but'. On 'I'd LIKE to…', which tone does she use: fall, rise or fall-rise? Write it.
assessment.rubric: Correct: fall-rise (I'd LIKE to… ↘↗ = I'd like to, but…: the voice goes down on LIKE and up at the end, so her manager hears that she isn't finished). 'fall' = 0 (a clear fall ↘ sounds like a plain yes, so the doubt disappears: the error this lesson targets). 'rise' = 20 (it sounds unsure, but more like a question than a hidden 'but').

assessment.prompt: Bu Ani watched Budi's presentation. His slides were excellent, but he spoke for far too long. She wants to hint at that politely, without saying it, with a fall-rise and extra stress on one word: 'Your slides were excellent… ↘↗'. Which word does she stress to point to the contrast? Write it.
assessment.rubric: Correct: slides (Your SLIDES were excellent… ↘↗ = the slides were; something else, his talk, wasn't. Budi fills in the 'but' himself). 'excellent' = 30 (a fall-rise there suggests 'excellent, but…' about the slides themselves, not the contrast with his talk). 'your' = 0 (it would contrast Budi's slides with someone else's). 'were' = 0 (it sounds like insisting against someone who said they weren't, or suggests they no longer are).

assessment.prompt: Dimas phones a hotel in Bali. The receptionist isn't a native speaker of English, and the line is noisy. He says: 'My booking number is 4 8 2 7 5 9.' Should he say the number faster, at the same speed or slower than the rest of his sentence? Write faster, same or slower.
assessment.rubric: Correct: slower (key numbers go slower than the rest of the sentence, in small groups with a short pause: four eight two | seven five nine; on a noisy phone line with a non-native listener even more so). An answer that adds 'in groups' or 'with pauses' = 100. 'same' = 0 (numbers are the easiest thing to mishear). 'faster' = 0 (the nervous habit this lesson targets).

assessment.prompt: Rina gives the same talk twice: first to six colleagues around a table, then to 400 people in a hall in Surabaya. In the hall, should her pauses be longer or shorter than in the small meeting? Write longer or shorter.
assessment.rubric: Correct: longer (in a big hall the sound travels and echoes, a large audience reacts more slowly, and key points need time to land, so she slows down and pauses longer). 'the same' = 20 (the small-room rhythm is too fast for a big hall). 'shorter' = 0.

assessment.prompt: Listen to Pak Hasan's question. In fact, the Bandung team finished the sales report last week. You correct him politely: 'Actually, the Bandung team finished it.' Which one word do you stress most? Write it.
assessment.listen: So the Surabaya team finished the sales report last week, right?
assessment.rubric: Correct: Bandung (he said Surabaya; the report and the time are right, so only the team name steps up: Actually, the BANDUNG team finished it. Said with a friendly voice, it sounds like a polite correction, not an accusation). 'team' = 30 (right area, but the word that tells the teams apart is Bandung). 'finished' = 0 (that would contrast finishing with something else, like starting). 'actually' = 0 (a softening word, not the correction).

blocks.text:
**Quick recap:** at B2 you met the fall-rise ↘↗ for doubt (*Really…? ↘↗*, like *Masa sih…?*) and a big jump up ↗ for surprise. At C1 you widened your pitch range and moved the stress to change the meaning (*I didn't say HE took the money*). Now you use all of that to show your **attitude** (sikap: what you feel about what you're saying).

**First, an honest note about the app.** Every recording here is **one calm computer voice reading plain text**. It can't sound sarcastic, doubtful or bored on purpose, and it doesn't put extra stress where we'd like it. So in this lesson the tune is **written in the text**, you say every example **out loud**, and the videos at the end let you hear **real** speakers.

**How we write the tune:**
- CAPITALS = the stressed, high word: *It MIGHT work*
- ↗ rise · ↘ fall · ↗↘ rise-fall (up, then down) · ↘↗ fall-rise (down, then up again) · → flat
- *Gre-eat* = the word is drawn out (diucapkan panjang)
- | = a pause

**Same kind of word, different attitudes:**
- **Real praise:** lively, a **wide** rise-fall with a high peak: *GREAT! ↗↘*
- **Sarcasm** (saying the opposite of what you mean): often **flat, low and drawn out**: *Gre-eat. →* Some speakers do the opposite and exaggerate wildly. Either way, the surest clue is that the words **don't fit the situation**.
- **Surprise:** fast, a big jump up: *You're moving to BALi?! ↗*
- **Boredom** (tidak tertarik): **narrow**, flat, low and short: *Oh. → Nice. →*
- **Warmth:** start a little higher, move gently, don't rush, soft fall: *It's SO good to see you. ↘* A smile really changes your voice: people can hear it.

**The Indonesian trap:** Indonesian often carries attitude in **words** (*kok, sih, deh, lho, masa*) and is usually spoken in a **narrower, flatter** range. In English the **voice** does that job. So a sincere *Great.* or *Congratulations.* said flat can sound **bored, or even sarcastic, by accident**. What feels 'lebay' to you usually sounds friendly and engaged to English ears.

These are strong tendencies, not laws: people, regions and situations vary.

id.text:
**Ulasan singkat:** di B2 kamu sudah bertemu nada turun-naik ↘↗ untuk ragu (*Really…? ↘↗*, seperti *Masa sih…?*) dan lompatan besar ke atas ↗ untuk terkejut. Di C1 kamu memperlebar rentang nada dan memindahkan tekanan untuk mengubah makna (*I didn't say HE took the money*). Sekarang kamu memakai semua itu untuk menunjukkan **sikap** (apa yang kamu rasakan tentang yang kamu katakan).

**Pertama, catatan jujur tentang aplikasi ini.** Setiap rekaman di sini adalah **satu suara komputer yang tenang, membaca teks biasa**. Suara itu tidak bisa sengaja terdengar menyindir, ragu atau bosan, dan tidak memberi tekanan ekstra di kata yang kita mau. Jadi di pelajaran ini nadanya **ditulis di teks**, kamu mengucapkan setiap contoh **dengan suara keras**, dan video di akhir pelajaran membiarkanmu mendengar pembicara **sungguhan**.

**Cara kita menulis nada:**
- HURUF BESAR = kata yang ditekan dan bernada tinggi: *It MIGHT work*
- ↗ naik · ↘ turun · ↗↘ naik-turun (naik, lalu turun) · ↘↗ turun-naik (turun, lalu naik lagi) · → datar
- *Gre-eat* = katanya diucapkan panjang
- | = jeda

**Jenis kata yang sama, sikap berbeda:**
- **Pujian tulus:** hidup, nada naik-turun yang **lebar** dengan puncak tinggi: *GREAT! ↗↘*
- **Sarkasme** (mengatakan kebalikan dari maksudmu): sering **datar, rendah dan panjang**: *Gre-eat. →* Sebagian orang melakukan kebalikannya dan melebih-lebihkan habis-habisan. Bagaimanapun caranya, petunjuk paling pasti adalah kata-katanya **tidak cocok dengan situasinya**.
- **Terkejut:** cepat, lompatan besar ke atas: *You're moving to BALi?! ↗*
- **Bosan** (tidak tertarik): **sempit**, datar, rendah dan pendek: *Oh. → Nice. →*
- **Hangat:** mulai sedikit lebih tinggi, bergerak lembut, tidak terburu-buru, turun pelan: *It's SO good to see you. ↘* Senyum benar-benar mengubah suaramu: orang bisa mendengarnya.

**Jebakan bahasa Indonesia:** bahasa Indonesia sering membawa sikap lewat **kata** (*kok, sih, deh, lho, masa*) dan biasanya diucapkan dengan rentang nada yang **lebih sempit dan datar**. Dalam bahasa Inggris, **suara**lah yang melakukan tugas itu. Jadi *Great.* atau *Congratulations.* yang tulus tapi diucapkan datar bisa terdengar **bosan, atau bahkan menyindir, tanpa sengaja**. Yang terasa 'lebay' bagimu biasanya terdengar ramah dan antusias di telinga penutur bahasa Inggris.

Ini kecenderungan yang kuat, bukan hukum: orang, daerah dan situasi berbeda-beda.

blocks.text: Say *Great* five ways into your phone: delighted, sarcastic, surprised, bored and warm. Wait a day, then listen without looking at your notes. Can you tell which is which? If the delighted one and the bored one sound alike, your range is too narrow: let your voice travel more.

id.text: Ucapkan *Great* dengan lima cara ke ponselmu: senang sekali, menyindir, terkejut, bosan dan hangat. Tunggu sehari, lalu dengarkan tanpa melihat catatanmu. Bisakah kamu membedakannya? Kalau versi senang dan versi bosan terdengar mirip, rentang nadamu terlalu sempit: biarkan suaramu bergerak lebih jauh.

blocks.prompt: Rina's colleague tells her he's just become a father. Rina is truly happy for him, but she says 'Congratulations.' in a narrow, flat, low voice →. What's the risk?
options: It can sound bored, or even sarcastic, although she means it.
It sounds too excited for an office.
blocks.explain: In English the voice carries the feeling. A narrow, flat, low *Congratulations* sounds bored or even sarcastic, the opposite of what Rina means. Warmth needs a little more height and movement; 'too excited' is the opposite problem.

id.prompt: Rekan Rina bercerita bahwa ia baru saja menjadi ayah. Rina benar-benar ikut senang, tapi ia mengucapkan 'Congratulations.' dengan suara yang sempit, datar dan rendah →. Apa risikonya?
id.explain: Dalam bahasa Inggris, suaralah yang membawa perasaan. *Congratulations* yang sempit, datar dan rendah terdengar bosan atau bahkan menyindir, kebalikan dari maksud Rina. Kehangatan butuh nada sedikit lebih tinggi dan lebih bergerak; 'terlalu bersemangat' adalah masalah sebaliknya.

blocks.text:
The **fall-rise ↘↗** (the voice goes down on the stressed word, then up again at the end) says **'I'm not finished: there's a but.'** It's the polite way to show doubt or **reservation** (keberatan halus) without saying the negative part:
- *It MIGHT work… ↘↗* = but I doubt it.
- *I LIKE it… ↘↗* = but… (I'm not sure it's right, I wouldn't buy it).
- *In THEORY, yes… ↘↗* = but in practice, no.

**The common error:** a **falling** tone ↘ on a doubtful sentence. *It might work. ↘* with a clear fall sounds like a calm, fairly sure statement, so your doubt disappears. Compare *It MIGHT work… ↘↗* (doubt) with *It WILL work. ↘* (sure).

**Contrastive stress + attitude.** At C1 the stressed word was the part you corrected (*I didn't say HE took the money*). With a fall-rise, the stressed word points to a contrast you **don't say**:
- *The FOOD was nice… ↘↗* = something else (the service? the price?) wasn't.
- *The DESIGN looks good… ↘↗* = other things (the price, the speed) don't.

The listener fills in the *but* themselves. That's why it sounds polite: you criticise without saying the critical words. It only works if the stress is clear: say every word equally (*I DIDN'T SAY SHE TOOK IT*) and there's no contrast and no hint. Stress only the word that carries it: *I didn't say SHE took it* (someone else did).

**The Indonesian trap:** in Indonesian you'd add words: *Bagus **sih**… tapi…*, *Bisa aja, **cuma**…*. In English the fall-rise does the job of *sih* and the unsaid *tapi*. Said with a flat, falling tune, the English words lose the hint.

At work, this is usually the best way to show doubt: a fall-rise plus a softening word (*might, quite, in theory*), not sarcasm.

id.text:
**Nada turun-naik ↘↗** (fall-rise: suara turun di kata yang ditekan, lalu naik lagi di akhir) berarti **'aku belum selesai: ada tapinya.'** Ini cara sopan untuk menunjukkan ragu atau **keberatan halus** tanpa mengucapkan bagian negatifnya:
- *It MIGHT work… ↘↗* = tapi aku ragu.
- *I LIKE it… ↘↗* = tapi… (aku tidak yakin ini tepat, aku tidak akan membelinya).
- *In THEORY, yes… ↘↗* = tapi dalam praktiknya, tidak.

**Kesalahan umum:** nada **turun** ↘ di kalimat yang ragu. *It might work. ↘* dengan nada turun yang jelas terdengar seperti pernyataan yang tenang dan cukup yakin, jadi keraguanmu hilang. Bandingkan *It MIGHT work… ↘↗* (ragu) dengan *It WILL work. ↘* (yakin).

**Tekanan kontras + sikap.** Di C1, kata yang ditekan adalah bagian yang kamu koreksi (*I didn't say HE took the money*). Dengan nada turun-naik, kata yang ditekan menunjuk ke kontras yang **tidak kamu ucapkan**:
- *The FOOD was nice… ↘↗* = ada hal lain (pelayanannya? harganya?) yang tidak.
- *The DESIGN looks good… ↘↗* = hal lain (harganya, kecepatannya) tidak.

Pendengar sendiri yang melengkapi *tapi*-nya. Karena itu terdengar sopan: kamu mengkritik tanpa mengucapkan kata-kata kritiknya. Ini hanya berhasil kalau tekanannya jelas: kalau semua kata sama kuatnya (*I DIDN'T SAY SHE TOOK IT*), tidak ada kontras dan tidak ada isyarat. Tekan hanya kata yang membawanya: *I didn't say SHE took it* (orang lain yang mengambil).

**Jebakan bahasa Indonesia:** dalam bahasa Indonesia kamu menambah kata: *Bagus **sih**… tapi…*, *Bisa aja, **cuma**…*. Dalam bahasa Inggris, nada turun-naik melakukan tugas *sih* dan *tapi* yang tidak diucapkan. Kalau diucapkan dengan nada datar dan turun, kata-kata bahasa Inggrisnya kehilangan isyarat itu.

Di kantor, biasanya inilah cara terbaik untuk menunjukkan ragu: nada turun-naik plus kata pelunak (*might, quite, in theory*), bukan sarkasme.

blocks.text: Practise with your hand: drop it on the stressed word and lift it a little at the end (↘↗). Then say the unspoken *but* sentence aloud once (*I LIKE it… but it's too expensive*), and once more without it. The second time, the tune alone should still carry the *but*.

id.text: Latihan dengan tanganmu: turunkan di kata yang ditekan dan angkat sedikit di akhir (↘↗). Lalu ucapkan sekali kalimat *tapi*-nya dengan keras (*I LIKE it… but it's too expensive*), dan sekali lagi tanpa kalimat itu. Pada kali kedua, nadanya saja harus tetap membawa *tapi*-nya.

blocks.prompt: Pak Hasan asks Dimas if the new app will be ready by June. Dimas thinks it's unlikely, but he doesn't want to say no directly. Which delivery shows his doubt?
options: It should be?! ↗ (a big jump up)
blocks.explain: A fall-rise on the stressed word leaves a *but* unsaid: it should be, but I doubt it. A clear fall sounds like a fairly confident yes, so the doubt disappears. A big jump up sounds surprised, as if Dimas has only just heard about June.

id.prompt: Pak Hasan bertanya kepada Dimas apakah aplikasi baru akan siap bulan Juni. Dimas pikir itu kecil kemungkinannya, tapi ia tidak mau langsung bilang tidak. Cara bicara mana yang menunjukkan keraguannya?
id.explain: Nada turun-naik di kata yang ditekan meninggalkan *tapi* yang tidak diucapkan: seharusnya bisa, tapi aku ragu. Nada turun yang jelas terdengar seperti 'ya' yang cukup yakin, jadi keraguannya hilang. Lompatan besar ke atas terdengar terkejut, seolah Dimas baru saja mendengar soal bulan Juni.

material.title: Hearing attitude: what to listen for

id.title: Mendengar sikap: apa yang perlu diperhatikan

blocks.text:
To hear someone's attitude, listen to **how** they say it, not only **what** they say. The main cues:
- **Pitch range:** wide and lively = engaged, pleased, surprised; narrow and flat = bored, tired, or sarcastic.
- **Length:** a key word drawn out (*Su-ure*, *Gre-eat*) often signals sarcasm or doubt; a very short, clipped word can sound impatient or cold.
- **The end of the tune:** a clear fall ↘ = finished and sure; a fall-rise ↘↗ = unfinished, a *but* is coming.
- **A pause before a word:** *It's… | interesting.* The speaker is searching for a polite word, which usually means reservation. This polite *interesting* is especially well known in British English.
- **A stressed word that sets up a contrast:** *The FOOD was nice… ↘↗*: so what about the rest?
- **Words vs situation:** a positive word about a bad situation (*Oh, lovely* when it starts to rain) is almost always sarcasm. This is the strongest clue, and it works even in a flat recording like the app's.

**Use several cues together.** One cue alone can mislead: someone may sound flat just because they're tired, or because that's how their accent sounds. If you're not sure, ask kindly: *Sorry, do you mean that, or are you joking?*

**The Indonesian traps, from the other side:**
- A narrow, flat range makes your own sincere praise sound bored or sarcastic, as you saw above.
- Ending a statement with a **rise** ↗ (*I finished the report ↗*) makes it sound like a question, or unsure, as if you're asking for permission. When you're sure, end with a clear **fall** ↘.
- In writing, all these cues disappear: *Great, thanks.* in an email can be read as sincere or as sarcastic. Add words that make it clear: *Great, thanks so much for the quick reply!*

id.text:
Untuk mendengar sikap seseorang, perhatikan **cara** ia mengatakannya, bukan hanya **apa** yang ia katakan. Petunjuk utamanya:
- **Rentang nada:** lebar dan hidup = antusias, senang, terkejut; sempit dan datar = bosan, lelah, atau menyindir.
- **Panjang kata:** kata kunci yang diucapkan panjang (*Su-ure*, *Gre-eat*) sering menandakan sarkasme atau ragu; kata yang sangat pendek dan terpotong bisa terdengar tidak sabar atau dingin.
- **Akhir nada:** turun yang jelas ↘ = selesai dan yakin; turun-naik ↘↗ = belum selesai, akan ada *tapi*.
- **Jeda sebelum sebuah kata:** *It's… | interesting.* Pembicara sedang mencari kata yang sopan, yang biasanya berarti keberatan halus. *Interesting* yang sopan seperti ini terutama terkenal dalam bahasa Inggris British.
- **Kata yang ditekan untuk membuat kontras:** *The FOOD was nice… ↘↗*: lalu bagaimana dengan yang lain?
- **Kata vs situasi:** kata positif tentang situasi buruk (*Oh, lovely* waktu hujan mulai turun) hampir selalu sarkasme. Ini petunjuk terkuat, dan tetap berlaku bahkan di rekaman yang datar seperti rekaman aplikasi ini.

**Pakai beberapa petunjuk sekaligus.** Satu petunjuk saja bisa menyesatkan: seseorang mungkin terdengar datar hanya karena lelah, atau karena memang begitu bunyi aksennya. Kalau tidak yakin, tanyakan dengan ramah: *Sorry, do you mean that, or are you joking?*

**Jebakan bahasa Indonesia, dari sisi sebaliknya:**
- Rentang nada yang sempit dan datar membuat pujianmu yang tulus terdengar bosan atau menyindir, seperti yang kamu lihat di atas.
- Mengakhiri pernyataan dengan nada **naik** ↗ (*I finished the report ↗*) membuatnya terdengar seperti pertanyaan, atau tidak yakin, seolah kamu minta izin. Kalau kamu yakin, akhiri dengan nada **turun** yang jelas ↘.
- Dalam tulisan, semua petunjuk ini hilang: *Great, thanks.* di email bisa dibaca tulus atau menyindir. Tambahkan kata yang memperjelas: *Great, thanks so much for the quick reply!*

blocks.text: Watch a short clip of a British or American TV comedy or interview with the sound on and the subtitles off. Each time someone says something positive, ask: real or sarcastic? Which cue told you: the range, the length, the end of the tune, or the situation?

id.text: Tonton klip pendek komedi atau wawancara TV Inggris atau Amerika dengan suara menyala dan subtitle dimatikan. Setiap kali seseorang mengatakan sesuatu yang positif, tanyakan: tulus atau menyindir? Petunjuk mana yang memberitahumu: rentang nadanya, panjang katanya, akhir nadanya, atau situasinya?

blocks.prompt: Dr. Wulan presents her research plan. A senior professor answers: 'Well… | it's certainly AMBITIOUS… ↘↗'. What is the professor most likely telling her?
options: He's very impressed and has no concerns.
He has doubts, probably about whether it can really be done.
He's surprised she has finished it.
blocks.explain: Three cues point the same way: the pause after *Well…* (searching for a polite word), the stressed *AMBITIOUS* (praise for one thing only) and the fall-rise (a *but* is coming: but can it be done?). Real enthusiasm would be wide and lively with a clear fall; surprise would be a fast jump up.

id.prompt: Dr. Wulan mempresentasikan rencana penelitiannya. Seorang profesor senior menjawab: 'Well… | it's certainly AMBITIOUS… ↘↗'. Apa yang paling mungkin ingin disampaikan profesor itu?
id.explain: Tiga petunjuk menunjuk ke arah yang sama: jeda setelah *Well…* (mencari kata yang sopan), *AMBITIOUS* yang ditekan (memuji satu hal saja) dan nada turun-naik (akan ada *tapi*: tapi apakah bisa dilakukan?). Antusiasme yang tulus akan lebar dan hidup dengan nada turun yang jelas; terkejut akan berupa lompatan cepat ke atas.

material.title: Fitting your delivery to the audience

blocks.text:
Good speakers don't have just one voice. They adjust five things to the room and the listeners: **pace** (tempo, how fast you speak), **volume**, **pausing**, **articulation** (how clearly you say each sound, especially word endings) and **formality of voice** (how relaxed or steady you sound).

**One rule always helps: slow down for key information.** Numbers, names, dates and your main point go slower than the rest, with a short pause before them: *Our budget is | four point two BILLion rupiah.*

**Situation by situation:**
- **Small meeting** (a few people around a table): natural conversational pace and volume; look at people and invite reactions.
- **Big hall or auditorium:** slower, with longer pauses (the sound travels and echoes, and a big audience reacts more slowly), a wider range and clearer stresses so the back row hears the key words. Keep the microphone at a steady distance; don't shout into it.
- **International, non-native audience:** a little slower, clear word endings, full forms (*going to*, not *gonna*), fewer idioms, no sarcasm, and a pause after each key point. This isn't talking down: it's how good international speakers sound.
- **Phone:** there's no face to read and the sound is thinner, so be slower and clearer than face to face. Say numbers in small groups (*0812 | 5567 | 3490*), spell names with words (*S for Surabaya*), and put your warmth in your voice.
- **Video call:** there's often a small delay, so pause a little longer before and after a question, let one person talk at a time, and don't jump in mid-sentence.
- **A child:** slower, simpler words, a warm and lively range, plenty of encouragement.
- **An elderly person:** slower and clearer; if they hear poorly, a little louder and a little **lower** in pitch (high sounds are usually the first to become hard to hear with age), and face them. Not baby talk, and not shouting: both sound disrespectful.

**The Indonesian trap:** nerves make many presenters speed up, drop word endings and flatten their range, especially in a second language. Plan where you'll slow down and pause, and mark it in your script. And remember that in English a steady, unhurried pace with clear falls sounds respectful and confident, the way *Bapak/Ibu* and polite words do in Indonesian.

id.text:
Pembicara yang baik tidak hanya punya satu suara. Mereka menyesuaikan lima hal dengan ruangan dan pendengarnya: **tempo** (seberapa cepat kamu bicara), **volume**, **jeda**, **artikulasi** (seberapa jelas kamu mengucapkan setiap bunyi, terutama akhir kata) dan **formalitas suara** (seberapa santai atau mantap suaramu).

**Satu aturan selalu membantu: perlambat untuk informasi kunci.** Angka, nama, tanggal dan poin utamamu diucapkan lebih lambat daripada bagian lain, dengan jeda pendek sebelumnya: *Our budget is | four point two BILLion rupiah.*

**Situasi demi situasi:**
- **Rapat kecil** (beberapa orang di sekitar meja): tempo dan volume seperti mengobrol biasa; tatap orangnya dan ajak mereka menanggapi.
- **Aula besar atau auditorium:** lebih lambat, dengan jeda lebih panjang (suara merambat dan bergema, dan audiens yang besar bereaksi lebih lambat), rentang nada lebih lebar dan tekanan lebih jelas supaya baris belakang mendengar kata kuncinya. Jaga jarak mikrofon tetap; jangan berteriak ke mikrofon.
- **Audiens internasional yang bukan penutur asli:** sedikit lebih lambat, akhir kata jelas, bentuk lengkap (*going to*, bukan *gonna*), lebih sedikit idiom, tanpa sarkasme, dan jeda setelah setiap poin kunci. Ini bukan meremehkan mereka: beginilah cara pembicara internasional yang baik terdengar.
- **Telepon:** tidak ada wajah yang bisa dilihat dan suaranya lebih tipis, jadi bicaralah lebih lambat dan jelas daripada bertatap muka. Ucapkan angka dalam kelompok kecil (*0812 | 5567 | 3490*), eja nama dengan kata (*S for Surabaya*), dan masukkan kehangatanmu ke dalam suara.
- **Video call:** sering ada sedikit delay, jadi beri jeda sedikit lebih lama sebelum dan sesudah pertanyaan, biarkan satu orang bicara pada satu waktu, dan jangan menyela di tengah kalimat.
- **Anak-anak:** lebih lambat, kata-kata lebih sederhana, rentang nada yang hangat dan hidup, banyak dorongan semangat.
- **Orang lanjut usia:** lebih lambat dan lebih jelas; kalau pendengarannya kurang baik, sedikit lebih keras dan sedikit lebih **rendah** nadanya (bunyi tinggi biasanya yang pertama sulit didengar seiring usia), dan hadapkan wajahmu kepadanya. Bukan bicara seperti kepada bayi, dan bukan berteriak: keduanya terdengar tidak sopan.

**Jebakan bahasa Indonesia:** rasa gugup membuat banyak presenter bicara makin cepat, menghilangkan akhir kata dan meratakan nada, apalagi dalam bahasa kedua. Rencanakan di mana kamu akan memperlambat dan memberi jeda, dan tandai di naskahmu. Ingat juga bahwa dalam bahasa Inggris, tempo yang mantap dan tidak terburu-buru dengan nada turun yang jelas terdengar hormat dan percaya diri, seperti *Bapak/Ibu* dan kata-kata sopan dalam bahasa Indonesia.

blocks.text: Before any talk or call, ask three questions: Who are they (native speakers or not, experts or not)? How big is the room? How will they hear me (in person, by phone, on video)? Then mark your script: slower here, pause here, louder here.

id.text: Sebelum presentasi atau panggilan apa pun, ajukan tiga pertanyaan: Siapa mereka (penutur asli atau bukan, ahli atau bukan)? Seberapa besar ruangannya? Bagaimana mereka akan mendengarku (langsung, lewat telepon, lewat video)? Lalu tandai naskahmu: lebih lambat di sini, jeda di sini, lebih keras di sini.

blocks.prompt: Budi is on a video call with a client in Surabaya. There's a delay of about a second, and he keeps talking over the client. What should he do?
options: Speak louder and faster, so he finishes before the client starts.
Pause a little longer before and after questions, and let one person talk at a time.
blocks.explain: With a delay, the client's answer arrives late, so Budi needs longer pauses and clear turns. Louder and faster makes the overlap worse. Switching off the camera doesn't fix the delay, and it removes the face that helps the client follow him.

id.prompt: Budi sedang video call dengan klien di Surabaya. Ada delay sekitar satu detik, dan ia terus bicara bersamaan dengan kliennya. Apa yang sebaiknya ia lakukan?
id.explain: Dengan delay, jawaban klien datang terlambat, jadi Budi perlu jeda lebih panjang dan giliran bicara yang jelas. Lebih keras dan lebih cepat justru memperparah tumpang-tindihnya. Mematikan kamera tidak menghilangkan delay, dan malah menghilangkan wajah yang membantu klien mengikutinya.

resources.title: English sarcasm - What They Really Mean
resources.note: A 3.5-minute BBC Learning English video (British English): Chloe says 'The British summer's fantastic, isn't it?' and Mark doesn't realise she's being sarcastic. It explains how, when and why some English speakers say the opposite of what they mean. Real voices, so you hear the sarcastic tone the app's voice can't produce.

Video ini menjelaskan bagaimana, kapan dan mengapa sebagian penutur bahasa Inggris mengatakan kebalikan dari maksudnya. Suaranya asli, jadi kamu mendengar nada sarkastis yang tidak bisa dibuat oleh suara aplikasi.

resources.title: Fall-Rise Intonation: English Pronunciation with Jennifer

resources.title: Intonation in English - English Pronunciation Lesson

Video ini membahas pola lebih detail daripada pelajaran ini; beberapa menit pertamanya yang paling berguna di sini.

id.intro: Di C1 kamu menaikkan kata kunci, memberi jeda untuk efek dan memindahkan tekanan untuk mengubah makna kalimat. Sekarang suaramu membawa sikapmu: pujian tulus atau sindiran, ragu dengan 'tapi' yang tidak diucapkan, terkejut, bosan atau hangat. Kamu juga belajar mendengar sikap itu pada orang lain dan menyesuaikan cara bicaramu dengan audiens. Satu catatan jujur: rekaman di aplikasi ini adalah satu suara tenang yang membaca teks biasa, jadi suara itu tidak bisa terdengar menyindir atau ragu. Nadanya ditulis di catatan, kamu mengucapkannya dengan suara keras, dan video di akhir pelajaran memberimu suara-suara asli.

assessment.pnat-1: Bu Ani mengumumkan bahwa rapat tim dipindah ke Sabtu pagi. Sari berkata: 'Wo-onderful. →' dengan suara rendah, datar dan panjang. Sikap apa yang ditunjukkan cara bicaranya? Pilih satu dari daftar ini dan tulis dalam bahasa Inggris: delighted, sarcastic, surprised.
assessment.pnat-2: Dimas bertanya kepada Pak Hasan: 'Will the client sign the contract this week?' Pak Hasan menjawab: 'I SUPPOSE so… ↘↗' (turun di SUPPOSE, lalu naik di akhir). Bagaimana perasaannya tentang hal itu? Pilih satu dari daftar ini dan tulis dalam bahasa Inggris: certain, doubtful, delighted.
assessment.pnat-3: Manajer Rina bertanya apakah ia bisa ikut makan malam dengan klien hari Jumat. Rina ingin ikut, tapi tidak yakin pekerjaannya bisa selesai tepat waktu, dan ia ingin manajernya mendengar 'tapi' yang tidak diucapkan itu. Untuk 'I'd LIKE to…', nada apa yang ia pakai: fall, rise atau fall-rise? Tulis jawabannya.
assessment.pnat-4: Bu Ani menonton presentasi Budi. Slide-nya bagus sekali, tapi Budi bicara terlalu lama. Bu Ani ingin menyiratkan hal itu dengan sopan, tanpa mengatakannya, dengan nada turun-naik dan tekanan ekstra pada satu kata: 'Your slides were excellent… ↘↗'. Kata mana yang ia tekan untuk menunjuk kontrasnya? Tulis katanya.
assessment.pnat-5: Dimas menelepon sebuah hotel di Bali. Resepsionisnya bukan penutur asli bahasa Inggris, dan sambungannya berisik. Ia berkata: 'My booking number is 4 8 2 7 5 9.' Apakah ia sebaiknya mengucapkan nomornya lebih cepat, sama cepat, atau lebih lambat daripada bagian kalimat lainnya? Tulis faster, same atau slower.
assessment.pnat-6: Rina memberikan presentasi yang sama dua kali: pertama untuk enam rekan di sekitar meja, lalu untuk 400 orang di sebuah aula di Surabaya. Di aula, apakah jedanya sebaiknya lebih panjang atau lebih pendek daripada di rapat kecil? Tulis longer atau shorter.
assessment.pnat-7: Dengarkan pertanyaan Pak Hasan. Sebenarnya, tim Bandung yang menyelesaikan laporan penjualan minggu lalu. Kamu mengoreksinya dengan sopan: 'Actually, the Bandung team finished it.' Kata mana yang paling kamu tekan? Tulis satu kata.
